newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - Australian banks please investors, not customers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Australian banks please investors, not customers.

text.p: Australian banks are enjoying record profits and are pleasing shareholders with handsome dividends and soaring share prices.
But not everyone is happy, with both rural and urban customers complaining that they are being hurt by the banks' moves to lower their costs.
As banks bring in the era of electronic banking, closing branches as they go, customers are feeling alienated.
"People are worried about branch closures and using services electronically," said Gerard Thomas, policy officer at Australian Pensioners and Superannuants' Federation.
"We certainly think that money is going to go back under the bed," Thomas told Reuters.
Communities in Australia's vast rural areas are especially upset with the banks following the closure of many branches in country towns.
"The effect has been quite devasting," said Todd Ritchie, director of economic policy at the National Farmers Federation.
"In many ways the banks were the last thing keeping these communities alive," Ritchie said. He said some bank customers would have to drive 200 km (125 miles) if their local bank branch closed.
The 1,100-strong community of Merriwa in the Hunter Valley area north of Sydney will soon have just one bank. Not so long ago there were three.
"The country areas are suffering again while the big corporations pull out and concentate on the cities," complained Merriwa pensioner Mal Frame.
BANKS STILL HAVE AN IMAGE PROBLEM

Bank-bashing has long been a national sport in Australia. Criticisms are largely based on a perception that banks are part of a community service, like health and social services, banking analysts said.
Banks are one of Australia's biggest spenders on advertising with over A$150 million (US$117 million) spent annually on promoting their products and polishing their image.

"I think it is largely founded on the behaviour of the banks in the late 80s, early 90s and their complete disregard for customer relationships," said Mike Porter, national media manager at advertising firm Young and Rubicam.
Young and Rubicam is currently working on a survey on banks to update one taken in 1994 when less than one-third of the 1,500 people surveyed held banks in esteem.
"I would be very surprised if anything significant changed between 1994 and 1997," Porter told Reuters.
The industry is dominated by the "big four" -- National Australia Bank Ltd, Westpac Banking Corp, Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd and Commonwealth Bank of Australia.

Bank customers' ire was raised further last month when Colonial Bank doubled fees on its deposit and savings accounts less than a week after the release of a government commissioned inquiry into the nation's financial system.
The Wallis inquiry, led by businessman Stan Wallis, recommended that banks would be able to charge fees to reflect their costs.

Australians enjoyed free banking until about three years ago when banks started to introduce fees on transactions. This has run into much criticism from customers, who have been looking at other ways to do their banking.

Former bank customers have been moving over to Credit Unions, low cost financial service groups, over the past three years, said Vern Harvey, chief executive at industry body Credit Union Services Corp.
"I think a lot of people are still unhappy with their banks," Harvey told Reuters.
AUSTRALIAN CUSTOMERS PAY THROUGH HIGHER RATES
Bank customers around the world are experiencing bank rationalisation, branch closures, massive staff layoffs and electronic banking.

"It is all over the world. Australia is a bit more vocal about it because we are going through a dramatic change from no fees to significant fees," said Jeremy Pooley, a banking and finance partner at accountants Cooper & Lybrand.
"In reality people have had it pretty good for a long time, and people have been paying for it (service) through higher interest rate charges," Pooley said.
In recent years with new entrants in Australia's mortgage lending market, the new competition has sliced 200 basis points off banks' home lending rates.
However customers are likely to see more charges as banks prop up their profits under continued pressure on margins," banking analysts said.

"Bank profitability is comparable with other countries, but banks here have traditionally had higher margins and lower charges than other countries. So banks are now doing a balancing act on margins and charges," one banking analyst said.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
